# [NVIDIA]{.grad-soft}

Can machine learning beat naive baselines at predicting whether NVDA closes up or
down the next day?

::: {.notice}
**An experiment, not advice.** Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy or
sell anything. The calls below are published so they can be scored, not so they can
be followed.
:::

## Latest range {.section-title}

A separate question from direction: how big is the next session's move likely to
be? Each forecaster gives a range that is meant to hold the move four days out of
five. The first one shown is the simple baseline the others are measured against.

::::: {.band}

[A simulated strategy]{.eyebrow}

## Paper strategy {.section-title}

One fixed rule turns the calls above into a pretend position, so that they can be
scored as a whole. After each close it is either "Holding" NVDA for the next
session or "In cash". It is Holding only when at least four of the six models say
up and the volatility gate is open, meaning the simple baseline's forecast of the
next move is not unusually large. No money is involved, and it is not a signal to
follow.

The rule and the way it is scored were written down before any result was seen.
One thing about it was not neutral: the volatility gate was chosen knowing that
volatility is predictable, the one positive result on this page.

## Method {.section-title}

### The question

Each day after the close, every model and baseline makes one call: will the next session
close higher than this one? "Higher" uses the closing price adjusted for dividends
and splits, and a flat day counts as not up.

### The baselines

Three rules that need no learning, and that any model has to beat:

- **Always up.** NVDA has closed up on a little over half of all days, so this is
  right more often than a coin flip. Following it is the same as buying and holding.
- **Persistence.** Tomorrow will do what today did.
- **200-day average rule.** Up when the price is above its average of the last 200
  sessions.

### The models

- **Logistic regression**: a weighted sum of the features.
- **XGBoost**: boosted decision trees, which can pick up thresholds and
  combinations of features.
- **LSTM**: a small neural network that reads the last 20 sessions in order.

Each of the three also runs as a second version, marked "+ context". It has the
same settings and more inputs (described below), so comparing the two versions
shows what the extra inputs added. The "+ context" versions joined the log later
and have their own, shorter, record.

Each model's settings were fixed before it was tested and were not adjusted
afterwards to improve the result.

### The features

Twenty numbers describing recent price and volume behaviour, all computed from data
up to that day's close: returns over the last 1 to 21 sessions, how volatile the
last week and month were, two standard momentum indicators (RSI and MACD), how far
the price sits from its 10, 50 and 200-day averages, volume compared with its recent
average, the day's high-to-low range, and the day of the week.

The "+ context" versions get fifteen more: how the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and a
semiconductor index moved over the last 1 and 5 sessions, how NVDA did against each
of them over the last month, the level of the VIX and how it changed, and three
numbers about NVIDIA's financial results: whether any had been published yet, how
many sessions ago the latest came out, and whether they came out after that day's
close. Results count only if the SEC had accepted the filing by 8 pm New York time
that day, whatever time the call was actually written.

### The range

A second set of forecasters answers a different question: not which way, but how
far. Each one estimates how volatile the next session will be, and that estimate is
turned into a range meant to hold the session's move 80% of the time, with the
misses split evenly below and above.

- **Long-run average.** Volatility is always what it has been on average.
- **Last 21 sessions.** The spread of the last 21 daily moves.
- **Weighted recent average.** The same idea with newer moves counting for more.
  This is the simple baseline the models have to beat, and the range shown first.
- **Three-speed regression** and **XGBoost (volatility)**: two models that learn
  how the last day, week and month of moves relate to the next one.

The range is the forecast volatility times two numbers taken from past sessions
only, so it does not assume moves follow a bell curve. Afterwards the log records
whether the move fell inside the range, below it or above it, and nothing else
about the move.

### The paper strategy

A simulated position built from the calls, to score them as a whole. After each
close it is "Holding" NVDA for the next session when at least four of the six
models say up and the volatility gate is open; otherwise it is "In cash". The gate
is open unless the weighted recent average's volatility forecast is above the 80th
percentile of its own past values. The four-of-six and 80th-percentile settings
were fixed in advance and are not adjusted.

It is measured against holding the stock throughout. The main measure is
risk-adjusted return (the Sharpe ratio: average daily return divided by how much it
varies) after costs, with total return, worst fall and time in the market reported
beside it. The gate was chosen knowing that volatility is predictable, so the
backtest is kinder to it than a rule chosen blind would deserve.

Live, the log records only the state and the two things the rule looked at. If any
of the six models makes no call for a session, the strategy has no entry for it:
that session is counted as missed, left out of both the strategy and the
buy-and-hold comparison, and never filled in afterwards. Because the log holds no
returns, the live record is a count of sessions, not a return.

### The test

Testing is walk-forward. A model is trained on the first five years, makes its
calls for the next 21 sessions, is retrained with those sessions added, and so on to
the present. No call is ever made by a model that has seen that day or any day
after it. Automated tests replace all later data with nonsense and check that
earlier calls do not change.

### Costs and simulated returns

The simulated strategy holds the stock on days called up and holds cash on days
called down. Each change of position is charged 5 basis points (0.05%) of the
amount traded. Cash earns nothing in the simulation.

### Limitations

- **One stock, one period.** NVDA rose enormously over the tested years. A rule that
  simply stays invested was always going to be hard to beat here.
- **The backtest flatters.** It is where approaches get compared, so the live log
  is the stronger evidence, and it needs more than a year of calls to say much.
- **Prices, indices and dates only.** The models see price and volume history, and
  the "+ context" versions also see market indices and when results came out. None
  of them reads the results themselves, the news or anything about the business.
- **Simulated is not real.** No slippage, no taxes, no interest on cash.
- **A range is not a direction.** It says how far the move may go, both ways, and
  it is wrong by design one day in five.
- **The paper strategy is not a signal.** It is one rule, partly chosen with
  hindsight, built from models that did not beat always calling up. It is published
  to be scored.
- **The data source is unofficial.** Daily prices come from Yahoo Finance and are
  checked before use, but they are not guaranteed.
